Its sound is warm and full of national character, most striking in the high register, where it can produce clear and expressive notes. The instrument has a straight tubular design and a comparatively small resonating cavity, which makes its sound focused and compact rather than broad and open like a flute. Its range lies mainly in the middle and high register, the low register being limited. Its tone is neither as full and warm as a saxophone nor as soft and inward as a clarinet, but has the open-hearted quality of folk music. In traditional folk music the tilinkó is often used in the melodic part, and its distinctive sound blends well into the overall colour of a folk ensemble.

The tilinkó is an Eastern European folk aerophone of the flute type, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.111-1. It is a harmonic flute without fingerholes and can be seen as an early form of the dentsivka; the player covers the opening at the end of the pipe with a finger and changes the pitch by the strength of the breath. The body is usually of lime, elder, sycamore or willow, about 35 to 40 cm long and sometimes up to 60 cm. It is found in the folk music of Ukraine, Romania and Hungary, and it also appears, alongside the sopilka, in the Kalush Orchestra's 2022 song "Stefania".
蒂林科的發聲體為無指孔管身，屬氣鳴笛類，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號: The sounding body of the tilinkó is a pipe without fingerholes; it is an aerophone of the flute type, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.111-1. The source states only that the body is made of lime, elder, sycamore or willow; the mouthpiece, reed and other parts are not described. The pitch is changed by covering the opening at the end of the pipe with a finger and by the strength of the breath, so the material information is at present limited to the main body.
蒂林科起源於東歐，特別是匈牙利和羅馬尼亞地區，是一種傳統的民間打擊樂器。這種樂器: The tilinkó comes from Eastern Europe, especially Hungary and Romania, and is a traditional folk percussion instrument. The instrument consists of a wooden handle and hanging metal plates, and produces a clear, pleasant sound when shaken. It matured gradually in the folk music of medieval Europe, and was mainly used by herders and farmers in daily life.
隨著時間推移，蒂林科從純粹的實用工具演變為正式的樂器，廣泛應用於民俗慶典、宗教儀: In time the tilinkó moved from being a purely practical tool to being a formal instrument, widely used at folk festivals, in religious rites and to accompany folk dances. Its distinctive tone has given it an important place in Eastern European folk ensembles. From the nineteenth to the twentieth century, with the revival of national music, the tilinkó gradually entered academic music and was recorded and studied by ethnomusicologists. Today the tilinkó has become an important symbol of European folk culture, and it continues to play a part in folk performances and music festivals of many kinds.
